```r
pcaData <- plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = c("dex", "cell"), returnData = TRUE)
percentVar <- round(100 * attr(pcaData, "percentVar"))

ggplot(pcaData, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = dex, shape = cell)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = rownames(pcaData)), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  xlab(paste0("PC1: ", percentVar[1], "% variance")) +
  ylab(paste0("PC2: ", percentVar[2], "% variance")) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "PCA of samples by treatment (dex) and cell line",
    color = "Treatment",
    shape = "Cell line"
  )
```

A few notes on why it's built this way:

- **`plotPCA()` from DESeq2** does the actual PCA under the hood (it picks the top 500 most variable genes by default), so it stays consistent with the rest of your DESeq2-based workflow rather than pulling in `prcomp` separately.
- **Color = `dex`, shape = `cell`** directly answers your stated question — you can see at a glance whether treatment or cell line drives the separation on PC1/PC2.
- **`geom_text_repel`** labels each point with its sample name, matching the labeling style you already used in the sample-distance heatmap (`dex`-`cell` naming).
- `coord_fixed()` keeps the PC1/PC2 aspect ratio proportional to the variance explained, which is standard practice and avoids visually distorting the spread.

If you want to go a step further, you could also pull the underlying data with `returnData = TRUE` (already done above via `pcaData`) and check `percentVar` printed in text, or extend to PC3 with a manual `prcomp()` call if two components don't cleanly separate your groups — happy to add that if this first pass leaves it ambiguous.

```r
dds <- DESeq(dds)

# 1) size factors used to normalise for sequencing depth
sizeFactors(dds)

# 2) dispersion estimates - check the gene-wise vs. fitted trend
plotDispEsts(dds)

# 3) confirm the model was fit correctly - check the available coefficients/contrasts
resultsNames(dds)
```

Why it's one block instead of three separate calls:

- **`DESeq()`** is itself a wrapper around `estimateSizeFactors()`, `estimateDispersions()`, and `nbinomWaldTest()` — calling those individually would be redundant, so this keeps the pipeline as the single canonical call rather than reinventing what it already does internally.
- **`sizeFactors(dds)`** surfaces the per-sample normalization factors it computed, so you can eyeball whether any sample was scaled unusually (useful cross-check against your library-size bar plot).
- **`plotDispEsts(dds)`** is the standard DESeq2 diagnostic — you want to see gene-wise dispersion estimates shrink sensibly toward the fitted red trend line, with no wild outliers suggesting a QC problem.
- **`resultsNames(dds)`** confirms the model actually fit the coefficients you expect from `design = ~ cell + dex` (e.g. `dex_trt_vs_untrt`), which sets you up cleanly for `results()` and `lfcShrink()` in your next step.

Added as **Step 5**, right after your DESeq2 pipeline run:

```r
# extract results for the treatment effect: dex trt vs. untrt, adjusting for cell line
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("dex", "trt", "untrt"), alpha = 0.05)

# order by adjusted p-value (most significant genes first)
res <- res[order(res$padj), ]

summary(res)
head(res)

# shrink log2 fold changes for more stable, interpretable effect sizes
# coef name comes directly from resultsNames(dds) above
resLFC <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "dex_trt_vs_untrt", type = "apeglm")

resLFC <- resLFC[order(resLFC$padj), ]
head(resLFC)
```

Why it's structured this way:

- **`contrast = c("dex", "trt", "untrt")`** explicitly extracts the treatment effect while your `~ cell + dex` design adjusts for cell line automatically — this matches the biological comparison you defined back in Step 1.
- **`alpha = 0.05`** tells `results()` to optimize its independent filtering threshold around your actual significance cutoff, which makes the `summary()` output accurate rather than defaulting to the generic 0.1.
- **`lfcShrink(..., type = "apeglm")`** uses the `apeglm` package you already loaded at the top — it pulls noisy fold-change estimates (typically from low-count genes) toward zero, which prevents them from dominating downstream volcano plots or gene rankings.
- **`coef = "dex_trt_vs_untrt"`** is copied directly from the `resultsNames(dds)` output in Step 4, so the coefficient name is guaranteed to match what DESeq2 actually fit rather than being guessed.

This sets you up cleanly for a volcano plot or MA plot as a logical next step, if you want one.

Added as **Step 7**, right after your Ensembl-to-symbol annotation:

```r
volcanoData <- as.data.frame(resLFC)
volcanoData$gene <- rownames(volcanoData)

# drop genes with missing padj (independent filtering) or missing symbol
volcanoData <- volcanoData[!is.na(volcanoData$padj) & !is.na(volcanoData$symbol), ]

# classify each gene as up, down, or not significant
volcanoData$sig <- "NS"
volcanoData$sig[volcanoData$padj < 0.05 & volcanoData$log2FoldChange > 1] <- "Up"
volcanoData$sig[volcanoData$padj < 0.05 & volcanoData$log2FoldChange < -1] <- "Down"
volcanoData$sig <- factor(volcanoData$sig, levels = c("Down", "NS", "Up"))

# top 10 upregulated and top 10 downregulated genes, ranked by adjusted p-value
topUp <- volcanoData[volcanoData$sig == "Up", ]
topUp <- topUp[order(topUp$padj), ][seq_len(min(10, nrow(topUp))), ]

topDown <- volcanoData[volcanoData$sig == "Down", ]
topDown <- topDown[order(topDown$padj), ][seq_len(min(10, nrow(topDown))), ]

topGenes <- rbind(topUp, topDown)

ggplot(volcanoData, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = sig)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Down" = "#2166AC", "NS" = "grey70", "Up" = "#B2182B")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = topGenes,
    aes(label = symbol),
    size = 3.2,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    fontface = "italic",
    color = "black",
    box.padding = 0.4,
    segment.size = 0.3
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Differential expression: dexamethasone-treated vs. untreated",
    x = expression(log[2] ~ "fold change"),
    y = expression(-log[10] ~ "adjusted p-value"),
    color = NULL
  )
```

Why it's built this way:

- **Uses `resLFC`** (the shrunk log2FCs from Step 5) rather than raw `res`, since shrunken fold changes are the standard for publication volcano plots — they avoid dramatic x-axis outliers from lowly-expressed genes.
- **Significance thresholds `padj < 0.05` and `|log2FC| > 1`** are the conventional volcano cutoffs (2-fold change, 5% FDR) — dashed guide lines mark them visually so a reader doesn't need the legend to find the cutoff.
- **Top 10 up/down by `padj`** (not by fold change) picks the most statistically confident hits, which is generally the more defensible choice for publication — happy to switch the ranking to fold-change-based if that fits your story better.
- **`geom_text_repel`** (already loaded) keeps labels from overlapping, and `fontface = "italic"` follows standard gene-symbol typographic convention in figures.
- Color scheme (`#B2182B` red / `#2166AC` blue) is a colorblind-friendly diverging palette common in genomics figures, with grey for non-significant points so the signal doesn't get visually diluted.

One thing worth flagging: a few genes may have `NA` `symbol` even after mapping (multi-mapping or unannotated Ensembl IDs) — the filtering step above drops those before labeling so the plot doesn't break, but you may want to double check none of your top hits got excluded that way.

```r
# select top 30 most significant genes by adjusted p-value
topGenesHeatmap <- rownames(resLFC)[order(resLFC$padj)][1:30]

# pull their VST-normalized expression values
heatmapMat <- assay(vsd)[topGenesHeatmap, ]

# relabel rows with gene symbols where available, fall back to Ensembl ID otherwise
rownames(heatmapMat) <- ifelse(
  is.na(resLFC[topGenesHeatmap, "symbol"]),
  topGenesHeatmap,
  resLFC[topGenesHeatmap, "symbol"]
)

# annotate columns by treatment and cell line
annotationCol <- as.data.frame(colData(vsd)[, c("dex", "cell")])
rownames(annotationCol) <- colnames(heatmapMat)

pheatmap(
  heatmapMat,
  scale = "row",
  annotation_col = annotationCol,
  clustering_distance_rows = "correlation",
  clustering_distance_cols = "euclidean",
  color = colorRampPalette(rev(brewer.pal(9, "RdBu")))(255),
  fontsize_row = 8,
  main = "Top 30 differentially expressed genes"
)
```

Why it's built this way:

- **Uses `vsd`** rather than raw counts — same rationale as your PCA/sample-distance heatmap earlier: raw counts have mean-dependent variance, which would distort clustering and color scaling.
- **`scale = "row"`** z-scores each gene across samples, so a highly-expressed housekeeping-level gene doesn't visually dominate a lowly-expressed but strongly-regulated one — this is the standard convention for DE heatmaps.
- **Gene symbols on rows** (falling back to Ensembl ID if unmapped) makes the plot publication-readable, reusing the annotation you built in Step 6.
- **`annotation_col` with `dex` and `cell`** puts colored bars above the heatmap so you can visually confirm the same treatment/cell-line clustering pattern you saw in the PCA plot — a nice cross-check between the two views.
- Reuses your existing `pheatmap` + `RColorBrewer` pattern from the sample-distance heatmap (just swapped `"Blues"` for a diverging `"RdBu"` palette, which is more appropriate here since values are centered z-scores that can go negative).

30 genes is a reasonable default for readability — easy to bump the `1:30` up or down if you want a tighter or broader view.
